newsitem.title: GERMANY: German workers protest unemployment, rightist threat.
newsitem.headline: German workers protest unemployment, rightist threat.

text.p: More than 100,000 Germans demonstrated across the country on Thursday at May Day rallies, protesting against record unemployment and an accompanying rise in right-wing extremism.

As workers rallied, hundreds of neo-Nazis and dozens of left-wing extremists smashed windows and stormed through the northern town of Muenden, where right-wingers organised an unauthorised march after earlier being banned from Leipzig.

Trade union demonstrators in Berlin, Leipzig, Hamburg and other major towns, meanwhile, paraded through streets shouting slogans and waving banners that blamed Chancellor Helmut Kohl for Germany's 4.5 million unemployed, the highest total since Adolf Hitler came to power in the 1930s.
Speakers at the largest rally of some 20,000 in the historic eastern town of Leipzig said Germans should be wary of letting economic hardship lead to a repetition of history.

"Sixty years ago it was the Jews who were blamed for everything. Now it is apparently the turn of the Turks, the Africans or the asylum-seekers," said Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the huge IG Metall metalworkers and engineering union.
"But we must stop other groups being made scapegoats for a second time in Germany history," Zwickel said.
The crowd applauded as he said Kohl's government could not address the jobless crisis and should be dissolved.

Earlier, a clergyman who played a central role in the uprising of Leipzig against the former communist rule in East Germany pleaded for peaceful solutions to the difficulties facing post-1990 unified Germany.

"Conflict, hate and violence threaten our lives," Pastor Christian Fuehrer told a crowded prayer meeting in the Nikolaikirche, the 12th century church which was the focus of famous "Monday demonstrations" of East Germans in 1989.
"The young are dissatisfied with their lives in our country... In their disappointment they are open to dangerous words, the ideology of violence and the grand promises of charlatans," Fuehrer said.

Earlier, around 150 left-wing extremists on the outskirts of Leipzig hurled rocks and fireworks at police who were trying to keep them apart from a small group of skinheads defying a ban on a rally there.
Other extremists of the left hurled bottles and stones at police in Berlin, where some 6,000 people took part in two revolutionary demonstrations.
But the worst violence was in the small tourist resort of Muenden, where police said they detained 150 people in clashes between right-wing and left-wing extremists.

Opposition politicians around the country used the May Day demonstrations to attack Kohl's government for its failure to reduce unemployment and accused it of widening divisions in society between rich and poor.
Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told the Leipzig demonstration it was time to reassess how Germany's wealth was being divided up.
It was a scandal that, while many in Germany were on million-mark salaries, pensioners had to make do with as little as 800 marks ($460) a month, he said.

Government politicians were swift to issue statements defending their record and countering that Lafontaine's party was slowing down economic growth by continuing to block a major tax reform planned for 1999.

"A liberating jolt of Germany is only possible when the opposition and the unions take off their brakes. Our (tax) plans have been on the table for 100 days. We are ready to talk and compromise," Finance Minister Theo Waigel said.
